title: Setting Up Your Lab
sub: Terminal, zsh, Homebrew, Python, PyCharm and the ~/lab practice folder
goals: Configure Terminal and confirm that the shell is zsh
Install the Xcode command line tools and Homebrew, and put Homebrew on your PATH
Install the networking and text tools the book uses with one brew command
Create a PyCharm project with its own virtual environment and run a Python file two ways
Create ~/lab with the Lab Kit and fill in My Values from your own network

blocks.text: In this chapter you will build the workbench for everything that follows: a configured Terminal running zsh, a package manager that installs tools in one line, a Python you control, an editor that runs it, and a folder of practice files. The chapter is mostly installation, so it moves briskly, but each step explains what the installer actually does to your Mac, because you will meet the same mechanisms (the `PATH`, startup files, virtual environments) in every later chapter.

Plan for about 40 minutes, most of it downloads. Open this page next to Terminal so you can copy commands across. Where a step needs your administrator password, Terminal prints no characters while you type it. That is normal, not a freeze.

The book targets Apple Silicon Macs (M1 and later) on macOS 13 or newer. macOS 26 Tahoe is the last release for Intel Macs; macOS 27 and later run only on Apple Silicon. Homebrew installs into `/opt/homebrew` there. On an Intel Mac the prefix is `/usr/local`, and every `/opt/homebrew` path below becomes `/usr/local`. Find out which you have with `uname -m`: `arm64` is Apple Silicon, `x86_64` is Intel. Homebrew 5 stopped testing on macOS 13 in November 2025, so macOS 14 or newer is the comfortable minimum. Homebrew also stops building new Intel packages from September 2026 and plans to stop running on Intel Macs from September 2027, which is one more reason the book assumes Apple Silicon.
Terminal

**Terminal** is an app that draws a window of text and forwards your keystrokes to a program called a **shell**. Open it with [[⌘Space]], typing `Terminal` and pressing Return, or from `/Applications/Utilities/Terminal.app`. Drag it to the Dock; you will use it constantly.
A new window prints a prompt like this:

blocks.code:
you@MacBook-Pro ~ %
  │   │            │ └─ prompt character: % means a normal user (# would mean root)
  │   │            └─── current directory; ~ is shorthand for your home folder
  │   └──────────────── this computer's name
  └──────────────────── your account name

blocks.text: You type a command after the `%` and press [[Return]]. The shell runs it, prints the output, and shows a new prompt.
Make it comfortable
Open **Terminal > Settings** ([[⌘,]]) and spend two minutes on these:

items.text: **Profiles > Text**: choose a monospaced font and a size you can read for hours. [[⌘+]] and [[⌘-]] change the size of the current window at any time.
**Profiles**: pick a dark profile if you prefer one. Select it and press **Default**.
**Profiles > Keyboard**: tick **Use Option as Meta key**. Without it, the word-jumping shortcuts in [zsh basics](#zsh-basics) ([[⌥B]] and [[⌥F]]) print odd characters instead of moving the cursor.
**General**: leave the shell on **Default login shell**. That is zsh on any current Mac.

blocks.text: Two details save time. Dragging a file or folder from Finder onto the Terminal window pastes its full, correctly escaped path. Holding [[Option]] and clicking inside a command you are editing moves the cursor there.
The shell: confirm zsh
Terminal is the window. The program inside it that reads your lines is the shell, and on macOS since Catalina the default is **zsh**. Check what you have:

blocks.code:
$ echo $SHELL
/bin/zsh
$ zsh --version
zsh 5.9 (arm64-apple-darwin24.0)
$ echo $0
-zsh

blocks.text: `$SHELL` is your configured login shell. `echo $0` prints the name the running shell was started with; the leading `-` is the traditional marker for a **login shell**, which is how Terminal starts zsh. The distinction matters in a moment, because login shells read a different startup file from other shells.
If `echo $SHELL` shows `/bin/bash`, a very old setup is still in effect. Switch with `chsh -s /bin/zsh` (it asks for your password), then open a new Terminal window.

blocks.name: echo (first look)
blocks.sum: Print its arguments to the terminal, separated by single spaces, followed by a newline.

how.text: `echo` is the simplest way to see what the shell has done to your command line. The shell expands variables (`$HOME`), command substitutions (`$(date)`), tildes and wildcards first, then passes the finished words to `echo`, which prints them. Because the shell splits the line into words before `echo` runs, multiple spaces between words collapse into one unless the argument is quoted.

In zsh, `echo` is a builtin that interprets backslash escapes (`\n`, `\t`) by default. Other shells and the separate `/bin/echo` program differ, so use `printf` when a script has to behave identically everywhere.

flags.d: Do not print the trailing newline.
Interpret backslash escapes (already the default in zsh; accepted for bash compatibility).
Do not interpret backslash escapes, printing `\n` literally.

gotchas: Unquoted `echo $PATH` and quoted `echo "$PATH"` look the same, but quoting matters as soon as a value contains spaces or wildcard characters.
Whether `-e` and backslash escapes work depends on the shell and on whether you run the builtin or the separate `/bin/echo` program. A script that must behave the same everywhere should use `printf`.

blocks.text: Xcode command line tools

macOS ships without a compiler, `git` or `make`. Apple packages those as the **Command Line Tools** (CLT), a roughly one to two gigabyte download that includes `clang`, `git`, `make` and the system headers. You do not need the full Xcode app, which is many times larger.

blocks.code:
$ xcode-select -p
/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools

blocks.text: If the tools are missing, the command fails instead:

blocks.code:
$ xcode-select -p
xcode-select: error: unable to get active developer directory, use `sudo xcode-select --switch path/to/Xcode.app` to set one (or see `man xcode-select`)

blocks.text: Install them with `xcode-select --install`, which opens a macOS dialog (click **Install**, accept the license, wait for the download). The Homebrew installer installs them for you if they are missing, so this step only lets you watch it happen on its own.

blocks.name: xcode-select
blocks.sum: Show, install or switch the folder that holds Apple's developer tools.

how.text: Many developer commands in `/usr/bin` (`git`, `clang`, `make`, and Apple's `python3`) are small stubs. When you run one, the stub asks `xcode-select` where the active developer directory is, then launches the real tool from there. With the Command Line Tools installed that directory is `/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools`; with full Xcode it can be inside `Xcode.app`.

`--install` starts the graphical installer for the Command Line Tools. If a stub finds no developer directory, macOS offers to run that installer for you, which is why a first `git` can pop up a dialog.

flags.d: Open the dialog that installs the Command Line Tools.

Forget a manual choice and return to the default selection (needs `sudo`).

examples.desc: Check whether the tools are installed

keep names that start with any of these four words

gotchas: After a major macOS upgrade, commands such as `git` can fail with `xcrun: error: invalid active developer path`. The old tools no longer match the new system. Run `xcode-select --install` again, or install the update from System Settings > General > Software Update.

blocks.title: The stub that points at Apple's Python

blocks.text: `/usr/bin/python3` exists on a fresh Mac, but it is only a stub. Running it without the Command Line Tools triggers the same install dialog, and with them it runs a Python that Apple uses for its own tooling. You will install a separate Python below and leave Apple's alone.
Homebrew

**Homebrew** is a package manager: one command downloads a tool, its dependencies and the instructions to wire them in. It keeps everything under a single prefix, `/opt/homebrew` on Apple Silicon, so it never overwrites anything Apple ships and you can remove it cleanly. Two kinds of package exist:

items.text: A **formula** is a command-line tool or library, usually a prebuilt binary called a **bottle** (`jq`, `nmap`, `python@3.15`).
A **cask** is a macOS application installed into `/Applications` (`pycharm`, `wireshark-app`).

blocks.text: Install it

The installer is a script you download and hand to `bash`. That pattern, `download | run`, is exactly what Rule 1 in the [Welcome](#welcome/rules) tells you to be careful with, so first read what you are about to run:

blocks.code: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh | less

blocks.text: Scroll with [[Space]] and quit with `q`. Nothing has been installed; you only displayed the script. Then run the official one-liner from [brew.sh](https://brew.sh):

blocks.code: /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

tokens.exp: the program that will interpret the installer (it is a bash script, even though your shell is zsh)
run the string that follows as commands
command substitution: run what is inside, paste its output here as one quoted word
fail quietly on HTTP errors instead of printing an error page into the script
but still show an error message if something fails
the script on Homebrew's GitHub repository

blocks.text: The script describes what it will do, waits for [[Return]], and asks for your password because it creates `/opt/homebrew`. When it finishes it prints **Next steps**. Run the two commands it shows (they are reproduced here), because a new shell does not know where `brew` lives yet:

blocks.code:
(echo; echo 'eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"') >> ~/.zprofile
eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"

blocks.text: The first command *appends* to `~/.zprofile` with `>>`. A single `>` would replace the file and discard anything already in it. Copy the block exactly. Redirection is explained in [Streams, redirection and pipes](#pipes).
What those two lines do:

items.text: `brew shellenv` prints shell commands that set environment variables: the Homebrew prefix, the folders to add to `PATH` (`/opt/homebrew/bin` and `/opt/homebrew/sbin`), the manual path and the zsh completion path.
`eval "$(...)"` makes the current shell execute that text now.

Appending the same line to `~/.zprofile` makes every future Terminal window do it automatically. Terminal starts a login shell, and a login shell reads `~/.zprofile` at startup. [zsh basics](#zsh-basics) covers all the startup files.

blocks.text: The exact lines vary between Homebrew versions, but the idea does not: it is plain text that changes your environment, so you can read it.
Verify the install in a new tab:

blocks.code:
$ brew --version
Homebrew 5.1.0
$ which brew
/opt/homebrew/bin/brew
$ brew doctor
Your system is ready to brew.

blocks.text: `brew doctor` checks for configuration problems and exits non-zero if it finds any. Warnings are advice, not emergencies; the [Fixes](#fixes) chapter covers the common ones.

blocks.name: brew install
blocks.sum: Download and install one or more formulae (command-line tools) or casks (applications).

how.text: `brew install` resolves the named formula, installs any dependencies it needs, downloads a prebuilt bottle (or compiles from source if none exists), unpacks it into `/opt/homebrew/Cellar/<name>/<version>/`, and creates symlinks in `/opt/homebrew/bin` so the command lands on your `PATH`. Because the prefix is user-writable on Apple Silicon, no `sudo` is needed after the first install.
Names that exist both as a formula and as a cask are ambiguous; `--cask` and `--formula` choose one. A cask downloads an application bundle (often a `.dmg`) and moves it into `/Applications`.

flags.d: Treat all named arguments as casks (macOS applications).
Treat all named arguments as formulae.
Show what would be installed without installing anything.
Print the verification and post-install steps.
Compile from source even when a bottle exists.

examples.desc: Install every package named in a text file, one per line

anat.exp: the names that follow are applications, not command-line tools

gotchas: A command that works in one Terminal tab but gives `command not found` in a new one usually means `brew shellenv` never made it into `~/.zprofile`.
Never run `brew install` with `sudo`. Homebrew refuses on purpose, because files owned by root in its prefix cause permission problems later.

blocks.text: The tool shelf
Install the whole book's toolkit with one command. Homebrew skips anything already present, so it is safe to run again.

blocks.code: brew install jq tree wget nmap mtr iperf3 httpie watch ripgrep fzf bat shellcheck tmux

blocks.text: Then install the packet analyzer, which is an application (a cask):

blocks.code: brew install --cask wireshark-app

blocks.text: Older tutorials say `brew install --cask wireshark`. The graphical app's cask is now `wireshark-app`, while the name `wireshark` refers to a command-line-only formula. The cask installs the app, command-line tools such as `tshark` and `capinfos`, and a helper that grants capture permission (ChmodBPF). Names change over time; if `brew install` reports that a name does not exist, run `brew search <word>`.

blocks.text: To confirm every tool landed on your `PATH`, ask the shell where each one is:

blocks.code: for t in jq tree wget nmap mtr iperf3 http watch rg fzf bat shellcheck tmux tshark; do command -v $t > /dev/null && echo "ok       $t" || echo "MISSING  $t"; done

blocks.text: `command -v name` prints where a command would run from and returns non-zero if it does not exist, which is what `&&` and `||` react to. The loop prints one line per tool.
Python
A Mac offers several Pythons, and mixing them up is the most common beginner snag. Know your options:

head: Source
What it is
Verdict for this book
rows: A stub into the developer tools, running an older Python that Apple uses for its own tooling
Do not use or modify it
The reference build from python.org, installed under `/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework`
Fine; run its `Install Certificates.command` once so HTTPS works
A formula (currently `python@3.15`) in `/opt/homebrew`, updated with `brew upgrade`
A virtual environment per project, created from a Python you already have
Used for every project in the book

blocks.text: Install the Homebrew one and check what the shell finds first:

blocks.code: brew install python

$ which -a python3
/opt/homebrew/bin/python3
/usr/bin/python3
$ python3 --version
Python 3.15.2
$ python3 -c 'print(2**100)'
1267650600228229401496703205376

blocks.text: `which -a` lists *every* match in `PATH` order, and the first is the one that runs. Homebrew's folder is ahead of `/usr/bin` because `brew shellenv` put it there. The last command is an early taste of Python's integers, which have no fixed size, unlike the 64-bit numbers a shell works with (see [How computers work](#computers)).
Why `pip install` fails globally
Homebrew's Python is marked as externally managed (PEP 668), so a bare `pip install` refuses to touch it:

blocks.code:
$ pip3 install requests
error: externally-managed-environment

× This environment is externally managed
╰─> To install Python packages system-wide, try brew install
    xyz, where xyz is the package you are trying to
    install.
    ...
hint: See PEP 668 for the detailed specification.

blocks.text: This protects Homebrew's own tools, which depend on that Python. The fix is a **virtual environment**: a private folder with its own `python` and its own packages. PyCharm creates one per project, and [Getting started with Python](#py-start) shows how to make one by hand.
PyCharm

PyCharm is a Python editor with a debugger, a test runner and a terminal built in. JetBrains now ships a single unified PyCharm: its core features, including Jupyter notebook support, are free, and the first launch starts a 30-day trial of the Pro features. When the trial ends the free core keeps working, and everything in this book uses only the free core.
Download it from [jetbrains.com/pycharm](https://www.jetbrains.com/pycharm/download/) and drag it to `/Applications`, or let Homebrew do it:

blocks.code: brew install --cask pycharm

blocks.text: Your first project

items.text: Set **Location** to a new folder in your home directory, for example `~/projects/hello-py`. Keep it **outside** `~/lab`, which the next section creates.

For the interpreter choose a **Project venv** (the default). PyCharm builds a `.venv` folder inside the project from a Python it finds, preferably the Homebrew one. Option labels differ slightly between PyCharm versions.
Create the project. PyCharm adds a sample `main.py`.

blocks.text: Run a file with the green triangle next to the code or the **Run** menu. The **Run** tool window at the bottom shows the exact command PyCharm used, which names the venv's Python, and ends with `Process finished with exit code 0`.
Three tool windows turn PyCharm into a complete workbench:

items.text: **Terminal** ([[⌥F12]]) opens a shell in the project folder with the project's venv already activated, so the prompt starts with `(.venv)`. Commands like `python3` and `pip` then act on the project, not the system.
**Python Console** is a REPL (an interactive prompt) running in the project's interpreter, useful for trying a line before writing it into a file.
**Packages** lists what is installed in the venv and installs more. **Settings > Project > Python Interpreter** shows which Python the project uses.

blocks.text: The Lab Kit below refuses to run if `~/lab` already exists, to protect your files. If you create that folder by hand, or let PyCharm create a project inside it, the kit stops with a message. Keep PyCharm projects in `~/projects` for now.
Create ~/lab with the Lab Kit

Every example in the book that needs data uses one set of files: a 120-line web server log, lists of IP addresses and hostnames, a CSV of users, a saved `ping` run, a saved `nmap` scan, and some small text files. The **Lab Kit** creates them in `~/lab` with a single paste, so your outputs match the ones printed in the book.

blocks.code:
~/lab
  ├── README.txt              what is here
  ├── access.log              120 web-server log lines (combined format)
  ├── ips.txt                 23 IP addresses, with duplicates
  ├── hosts.txt               10 domain names
  ├── users.csv               name,role,ip,port with a header row
  ├── ping.log                a saved macOS ping run, one lost probe
  ├── scan.txt                a saved nmap scan of five LAN hosts
  ├── notes.txt               free text with TODO and ERROR lines
  └── data/
      ├── alpha.txt  beta.txt  gamma.log  delta.log  report-2026-09.csv
      └── archive/old.log

blocks.text: Click **Copy the Lab Kit**, switch to Terminal, paste, and press [[Return]]. It prints `Lab ready:` when it is done. Your files go in your home folder, not on the Desktop or in Documents, because those folders may sync to iCloud and macOS asks for permission before Terminal touches them.
What the kit actually does

You are about to paste about 300 lines into your shell, so know what they are. Open **Read it before you run it** above to see the whole script. It is built from three ingredients: `mkdir -p` to create the folders, a function wrapper so nothing leaks into your shell, and one block like this per file:

blocks.title: One file of the Lab Kit

tokens.exp: the program that copies its standard input to its standard output
redirect that output into a new file with this name
a here-document: use the lines that follow, up to a line holding only PPP_EOF, as standard input
the closing marker; the quotes around the opening marker stop the shell from interpreting `$` or backticks inside the data

blocks.text: The kit contains no `sudo`, no download, no deletion and no network access. It only creates files below `~/lab`. If `~/lab` already exists it prints a message and does nothing, so it cannot overwrite your work. To start over, rename the old folder first with `mv ~/lab ~/lab.old` and paste the kit again.
Check the result:

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ ls
README.txt  access.log  data  hosts.txt  ips.txt  notes.txt  ping.log  scan.txt  users.csv
$ wc -l access.log
     120 access.log

blocks.text: My Values

You met the yellow placeholder chips in the [Welcome](#welcome/legend). Commands that need your own IP address, gateway or interface name use them, and **My Values** stores one answer for the whole book. Run the probe below from Terminal and paste its five output lines into the box.

The probe uses four small read-only commands that [See your own network](#net-local) explains in detail. In short: `ipconfig getifaddr en0` prints your IPv4 address, `route -n get default` describes the route your traffic takes to leave the network, `awk` picks the gateway and interface lines out of it, `scutil --dns` shows your DNS server, and `ifconfig en0` shows the hardware (MAC) address.

blocks.title: If a value comes back empty

blocks.text: The probe assumes your active connection is `en0`, which is Wi-Fi on most laptops. If you are on Ethernet, or not connected, a line may be blank. Run `route -n get default | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}'` to find the interface that carries your traffic (it may be `en1` or higher for an adapter), then edit the values by hand in the table. Any value you leave at its default still works for examples that do not touch your network.
A ten-minute tour

items.text: `pwd` prints the **working directory**, the folder commands act on by default. `~` is shorthand for your home folder.
`ls` lists a folder. `-l` shows one entry per line with permissions, owner, size and date; `-a` includes hidden entries (names starting with `.`), including `.` (this folder) and `..` (its parent).
`cd` changes directory. `cd ..` goes up one level and `cd -` returns to where you just were.

blocks.text: `cat` prints a whole file, `head -3` prints the first three lines, and `wc -l` counts lines. Finally, send a packet. `ping` asks another machine to answer, which tests whether it is reachable and how long the round trip takes.

blocks.code:
$ ping -c 3 example.com
PING example.com (93.184.216.34): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=0 ttl=56 time=29.318 ms
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=1 ttl=56 time=28.774 ms
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=2 ttl=56 time=30.051 ms

--- example.com ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 28.774/29.381/30.051/0.523 ms

tokens.exp: the program: sends ICMP echo requests and waits for replies
flag: stop after 3 probes (without it, ping runs until you press Ctrl+C)
argument: the machine to probe, by name or IP address

blocks.text: Your addresses and times will differ. The book's samples use `93.184.216.34`, the address `example.com` had for many years; it has since moved to new hosting, so a real `ping` or `dig` shows other numbers.

Each reply line shows the probe number (`icmp_seq`), how many routers the packet may still cross (`ttl`) and the round-trip time in milliseconds. The last line summarizes minimum, average, maximum and standard deviation. [How networks work](#networks) explains where each number comes from.

blocks.title: Stop a command that never ends

blocks.text: Run `ping example.com` with no count, watch a few replies, then press [[⌃C]]. The statistics print when ping is interrupted. If a program ever hangs, [[⌃C]] is the first thing to try.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Verify the toolchain

task.text: Print, one per line and in one command line, the version of zsh, Homebrew, Python and git, followed by the path of the developer tools directory. Every line should come from a real command, not from typing.

hints: Separate commands with `;`. Homebrew prints several lines; keep only the first with `head -1`.
`brew --version | head -1` and `git --version`; the developer path comes from `xcode-select -p`.
blocks.solution: zsh --version; brew --version | head -1; python3 --version; git --version; xcode-select -p

why.text: Each program reports its own version, and `;` runs them in sequence. If any line says `command not found`, that tool is missing or off your `PATH`: revisit the matching section of this chapter. This one-liner is also a useful diagnostic to paste when asking someone for help.

blocks.verify: command -v brew > /dev/null && command -v python3 > /dev/null && echo "OK: brew and python3 are on PATH"

blocks.title: Run the Lab Kit and count the log

task.text: Create `~/lab` with the Lab Kit, change into it, and print the number of lines in `access.log` so that only the number appears (no file name). Then print the number of entries in `data/`.

hints: `wc -l` prints the file name when given a file argument. Feeding the file on standard input removes it.
`wc -l < access.log` for the log; `ls data | wc -l` for the folder.
blocks.solution:
cd ~/lab
wc -l < access.log
ls data | wc -l

why.text: `wc -l < file` makes the shell open the file and feed it to `wc`, so `wc` never learns the name. On macOS `wc` pads its number with spaces; the arithmetic test in `verify` ignores them. The second command pipes a listing into a counter, the pattern that [Streams, redirection and pipes](#pipes) builds on.

blocks.title: One Python file, two ways

task.text: Create `hello.py` in your PyCharm project with the content below. Run it three ways: with PyCharm's Run button, with `python3 hello.py` in PyCharm's Terminal tool window, and with `python3 hello.py` in a separate Terminal tab (after `cd ~/projects/hello-py`). Compare the `exe:` line in all three outputs and explain any differences.

task.code:
import sys, platform
print("python:", sys.version.split()[0])
print("exe:   ", sys.executable)
print("mac:   ", platform.mac_ver()[0])

hints: `sys.executable` is the path of the interpreter that is running the code.
PyCharm runs your file with the venv's Python, and its Terminal tool window activates that venv. A separate Terminal tab does not.

why.text: PyCharm's Run button and its Terminal tool window both use the project's `.venv/bin/python`. A fresh Terminal tab uses whichever `python3` comes first in `PATH`, normally Homebrew's. All three are Python, but they are different interpreters with different installed packages. Knowing which one is running explains most "it works in PyCharm but not in Terminal" problems. You can always check with `python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)'`.

blocks.title: Break PATH on purpose, then fix it

task.text: Simulate a Mac whose shell never loaded Homebrew's settings. Run `brew --version` inside a clean zsh that starts with an empty environment and no startup files, and read the error and its exit status. Then run `brew` by its full path, then fix the clean shell by evaluating `brew shellenv` inside it.

hints: `env -i` starts a program with an empty environment, and `zsh -f` skips every startup file.
The full path of brew is `/opt/homebrew/bin/brew`. `-c 'commands'` runs commands and exits.

why.text: The first command prints `command not found: brew` and status 127, the shell's code for "no such command", because Homebrew's folder is not in that shell's `PATH`. The full path works because a command containing a slash is run directly, with no `PATH` search. The third command shows that one `eval` fixes the clean shell, which is exactly what your `~/.zprofile` line does at every login. The experiment cannot harm your real shell, since the clean zsh is a separate process that exits. On an Intel Mac, `brew` lives in `/usr/local/bin`, which zsh searches by default, so the first command succeeds there and the lesson is only visible on Apple Silicon.

blocks.verify: /opt/homebrew/bin/brew --version > /dev/null && echo "OK: brew works by full path"

blocks.title: Which python3 wins?

task.text: A shell prints this for `which -a python3`:
Which interpreter runs when you type `python3`? What would you change so that the Homebrew one runs, and how can you confirm the change worked?

hints: `which -a` lists matches in the order the shell searches the folders of `PATH`.
blocks.solution: The first line wins: /usr/local/bin/python3 (for example a python.org install). To prefer Homebrew, put /opt/homebrew/bin before /usr/local/bin in PATH (brew shellenv does this when it runs last in ~/.zprofile), or remove the older install. Confirm with: which python3 and python3 --version, or python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)'.

why.text: The shell walks `PATH` left to right and runs the first match, so order is everything. Several installers (python.org, Homebrew, version managers) each add a folder to the front, and the last one to run wins. `type -a python3` shows the same list. [How computers work](#computers) explains the lookup in detail.

questions.q: Which prompt character tells you the shell is running as a normal user and not as root?
questions.why: zsh's default prompt ends in `%` for a normal user and `#` for root. The `$` in this book's transcripts stands for the prompt but is never typed.

options.text: Runs the commands that `brew shellenv` prints, putting Homebrew on `PATH` in the current shell

questions.why: `brew shellenv` only prints environment settings as text. `eval` makes the shell execute that text, and the same line in `~/.zprofile` repeats it in every new login shell.

questions.q: Why does a plain `pip install requests` fail with Homebrew's Python?

options.text: The Python is marked externally managed (PEP 668), so packages go into a virtual environment instead

questions.why: Homebrew protects its own Python from global package changes. A virtual environment, such as the `.venv` PyCharm creates for each project, gives you a private place to install.

questions.q: Which flag of `brew install` shows what would happen without installing anything?
questions.why: `-n` or `--dry-run` previews the install, which is useful before a large package.

questions.q: The Lab Kit prints a message and does nothing. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: `~/lab` already exists, and the kit refuses to overwrite it

questions.why: The kit is designed to stop rather than touch an existing folder. Rename the old one with `mv ~/lab ~/lab.old` and run it again.

questions.q: `which -a python3` lists `/opt/homebrew/bin/python3` first and `/usr/bin/python3` second. Which one runs?
questions.why: The shell runs the first matching program it finds while scanning the folders of `PATH` from left to right.
